The assassination achieves its objective, yet it gives the occupation authorities the occasion for indiscriminate vengeance against prisoners, resistance contacts, and communities with no connection to the attack.

The Nazis answer Heydrich's death with executions, terror, and the destruction of Lidice. Rewards and threats close around the underground network. Karel Čurda, one of the returned parachutists, goes to the Gestapo and identifies people who helped the soldiers. The trail leads to the Moravec family and, through brutal interrogation, toward the Orthodox church in Prague where the wanted men have taken refuge. The church's priests and lay supporters are now endangered along with the fighters they shelter.

German forces surround the church. Opálka, Kubiš, and another defender fight from the gallery until they are killed or fatally wounded. Gabčík, Valčík, and the remaining parachutists hold the crypt below as the attackers use gunfire, gas, and water in an attempt to drive them out. Escape proves impossible, and the defenders die without surrendering. The resistance network and the church community pay heavily, as do civilians swept up in the reprisals. Returning to the problem that has interrupted him throughout, the narrator acknowledges that facts cannot restore the dead or grant access to their private minds. He ends by affirming the parachutists' courage and the importance of remembering their choice without pretending that fiction can possess them.

characters.description: The owner of a struggling London record shop, in his mid-thirties and newly left by his girlfriend Laura. He organizes experience through records, lists, and carefully judged taste, but is much less disciplined about work or intimacy. Her departure sends him back through the history of his most painful breakups in search of an explanation.
characters.name: Rob Fleming

characters.description: Rob's girlfriend at the start of the breakup. She is a lawyer with a demanding career and has shared a home with him. She has just left, but their money, belongings, and long history keep the separation from being clean or final.
characters.name: Laura

characters.description: One of Rob's two employees at the record shop. Loud, argumentative, and merciless about other people's musical taste, he turns ordinary shop conversations into performances and disputes.
characters.name: Barry

characters.description: Rob's quieter employee and fellow music obsessive. Reserved and socially awkward, he usually yields space to Barry's noise but has interests and abilities that Rob has barely bothered to notice.
characters.name: Dick

characters.description: A man who once lived upstairs from Rob and Laura and has now become part of Laura's life. His interest in spiritual practices and calm self-presentation make him an especially irritating rival in Rob's imagination.
characters.name: Ian

characters.description: Laura's close friend, who also knows Rob well enough to confront him. She is protective of Laura but remains one of the few people willing to tell Rob what is actually happening rather than indulge his preferred version.
characters.name: Liz

characters.description: An American singer-songwriter visiting London. Rob admires her records before meeting her, then discovers a direct and approachable person behind the breakup songs he has treated as emotional evidence.
characters.name: Marie LaSalle

characters.description: Rob's earliest girlfriend and the first name on his private list of defining breakups. Their school-age relationship ended abruptly, leaving him with an old story about rejection that he has never checked against adult reality.
characters.name: Alison Ashworth

characters.description: One of Rob's teenage girlfriends. He remembers her mainly through his own sexual frustration and the grievance he constructed when their relationship ended.
characters.name: Penny Hardwick

characters.description: A former girlfriend included in Rob's list of major romantic injuries. His recollection treats the breakup as something done to him, a version he intends to revisit.
characters.name: Jackie Allen

characters.description: A glamorous former girlfriend whose sophistication made Rob feel admitted to a more exciting social world. Her later rejection remains central to his sense that he has repeatedly been judged inadequate.
characters.name: Charlie Nicholson

characters.description: The former partner Rob lived with before Laura. Their relationship began when both were recovering from rejection, and he remembers its ending as another item in his record of abandonment.
characters.name: Sarah Kendrew

characters.description: One of two teenagers caught stealing from Rob's shop. His abrasive manner gives Rob little reason to expect that he has any serious musical ambition.
characters.name: Vince

characters.description: Vince's companion in shoplifting and music-making. Along with Vince, he forces Rob to look beyond the pair's petty theft and listen to what they have created.
characters.name: Justin

recaps.ending: Laura's father's death interrupts the couple's cycle of accusation and avoidance. Rob attends the funeral and supports Laura, and their intimacy resumes, though neither pretends that grief alone has repaired the relationship. Laura ultimately chooses to be with him and asks him to consider marriage, while Rob confronts his habit of treating every new attraction as proof that a better life might be elsewhere. He does not become instantly certain or transformed, but he begins choosing the relationship he actually has. His working life also opens outward: the music made by Vince and Justin gives him a chance to start a small label, and Laura organizes a night at which he DJs. Dick and Barry reveal lives and talents beyond the narrow roles Rob assigned them. In the closing movement, Rob starts making a compilation tape for Laura and, for once, shapes it around what she would want rather than using it solely to display himself. He and Laura are back together with commitment under active consideration, and Rob has begun exchanging endless imagined alternatives for imperfect, deliberate participation in love and work.
recaps.in_short: When Laura leaves him, London record-shop owner Rob Fleming responds by ranking his five worst breakups and tracking down the women involved. The interviews overturn his cherished identity as a serial victim: some relationships were trivial, and in others he caused the hurt or ignored what his partners needed. While obsessing over Laura's relationship with their former upstairs neighbor Ian, Rob sleeps with musician Marie LaSalle and continues imagining that a different woman will fix him. His shop employees Dick and Barry, and two young shoplifters whose record he decides to release, reveal possibilities beyond his stagnant routine. The death of Laura's father brings Rob and Laura back into honest contact. They resume their relationship, discuss marriage, and accept that commitment is a choice rather than certainty that no alternative could be better. Laura arranges a DJ night for him, and Rob ends by making her a tape guided by her tastes, a small sign that he is learning to direct attention beyond himself.

recaps.text: Laura has left Rob Fleming, ending their years of living together and sending him into an audit of his romantic past. Rob owns a small London shop that sells carefully selected records and spends his days with Dick and Barry, two employees whose musical judgments are as intense as his own. Rather than examine Laura's complaints about his passivity, Rob compiles a list of the five breakups that hurt him most: Alison Ashworth, Penny Hardwick, Jackie Allen, Charlie Nicholson, and Sarah Kendrew. He treats the list as evidence that rejection is something women repeatedly do to him. Laura's move toward Ian, a former upstairs neighbor whom Rob despises, deepens his humiliation. Conversations with Laura and her friend Liz make clear that the breakup has causes Rob would prefer not to face, while his record collecting and rankings provide a familiar refuge.

Rob begins contacting the women on his list, claiming that he wants to understand why his relationships fail. The inquiries quickly disturb the tidy story he has preserved. His earliest romance with Alison was a brief school relationship rather than a permanent wound, and the adult lives of his former partners did not remain suspended at the moment they left him. Penny explains the pain behind behavior Rob remembered only as sexual rejection. Jackie reverses another grievance by pointing out that Rob was the one who ended their relationship. These encounters show how consistently he has edited the past to protect his self-image. At the same time he remains preoccupied with Laura and Ian, calling, questioning friends, and trying to learn details that cannot make him feel better.

The later stops in Rob's romantic investigation continue to weaken his mythology. Charlie, whom he remembered as glamorous and devastating, no longer seems like the ideal against which his life should be measured. His relationship with Sarah is revealed as a bond between two insecure people rather than a simple story of abandonment. Rob also meets the American musician Marie LaSalle, whose songs he admires. Their attraction leads to sex, but the encounter does not resolve his attachment to Laura or alter the habits that damaged the relationship. Dick and Barry continue running the shop with him, their own interests emerging whenever Rob pays attention. His search has produced information, but its clearest lesson is one he resists: the common factor in the failed relationships is not merely the women who left.

Rob's fixation on Ian turns jealousy into surveillance and fantasy, though direct encounters make the rival less powerful than the version in Rob's head. Laura remains connected to Rob through shared money, history, and unresolved feeling, but she will not simply return to the unchanged relationship. At the shop, Rob catches teenagers Vince and Justin stealing records and then learns that they make music themselves. Their rough recording gives him the idea of releasing a single, a modest project that could turn his expertise into something more constructive than criticism. The possibility arrives alongside further evidence that Dick and Barry have private ambitions and relationships Rob barely knows about. His life is not as fixed as he assumes, but movement requires him to invest in people rather than classify them.

Laura's father dies, shifting attention away from Rob's romantic scorekeeping. Rob attends the funeral and supports Laura through her grief. Their renewed closeness leads them back into a sexual relationship, but both know that returning to bed does not erase the reasons she left. The death and the family gathering force Rob to encounter adult responsibility without turning it into a list or an argument about taste. He begins to recognize that his constant readiness to imagine another woman has kept him only partly present in every relationship. Laura, exhausted by upheaval but still attached to him, is willing to consider rebuilding if he can choose participation over endless comparison. The small record-label idea involving Vince and Justin also moves forward, offering Rob a way to create rather than merely judge.

Rob and Laura resume their relationship without claiming that either certainty or perfection has suddenly arrived. Laura raises the possibility of marriage, and Rob tries to understand commitment as a decision made despite the existence of other attractive people, not as proof that alternatives have vanished. She organizes an event where he can DJ, reconnecting him with the pleasure and competence that first shaped his working life. Dick and Barry display musical and personal dimensions that Rob had overlooked, while the proposed release for Vince and Justin gives the shop a creative future. Rob still notices other women and remains prone to self-absorption, but he no longer treats every passing possibility as a command to leave. As he begins a new compilation tape for Laura, he considers her preferences and the effect of the music on her. That change of audience marks his tentative shift from self-display toward mutual attention.

characters.description: A Trenton apprehension agent whose persistence still exceeds her formal skill. Her apartment and routines are recovering from the upheaval of her last case. Her relationship with Joe Morelli has become physical but remains undefined, while Ranger is still her professional mentor and an equally unsettling source of attraction.
characters.name: Stephanie Plum

characters.description: A Trenton police officer and Stephanie's intermittent lover. He wants a more orderly place in her life than her work or her independence readily permits, and he regards Ranger as both a practical danger and a personal rival.
characters.name: Joe Morelli

characters.description: Vinnie's most capable apprehension agent and Stephanie's mentor. He begins offering Stephanie well-paid work outside her ordinary bond files without explaining much about it. Their professional trust is accompanied by an attraction neither treats as entirely theoretical.
characters.name: Ranger

characters.description: A former street worker who is now part of Vinnie's office and Stephanie's usual field partner. She brings confidence, local knowledge, and enthusiasm to surveillance and apprehensions.
characters.name: Lula

characters.description: Stephanie's grandmother, an energetic observer of neighborhood scandal and police activity. A disappearance within the family gives her a direct reason to join Stephanie's questions.
characters.name: Grandma Mazur

characters.description: Stephanie's cousin and the owner of Vincent Plum Bail Bonds, who supplies her fugitive files while trying to protect the agency's money.
characters.name: Vinnie Plum

characters.description: The bail-bond office manager who controls the files and keeps the agency functioning. She gives Stephanie practical information and draws on extensive Trenton connections.
characters.name: Connie Rosolli

characters.description: Stephanie's habitually frugal uncle, whose dispute over a refuse bill is followed by his unexplained disappearance. His ordinary routines leave the family with few obvious reasons for him to vanish voluntarily.
characters.name: Uncle Fred

characters.description: Fred's wife and Stephanie's aunt. Alarmed when her husband does not return, she asks the family for help and supplies Stephanie with the details of his recent habits and complaints.
characters.name: Aunt Mabel

characters.description: A small, sharp-tongued computer programmer who has failed to appear in court. He is Stephanie's paying fugitive assignment and proves difficult to manage even after she locates him.
characters.name: Randy Briggs

characters.description: A persistent man asking questions about Fred and presenting himself as someone with a financial interest in finding him. His attention makes clear that the missing man had contacts his family did not know about.
characters.name: Bunchy

characters.description: An easygoing young Trenton resident whose unconventional circle becomes useful to Stephanie during the search.
characters.name: Mooner

characters.description: Mooner's friend and companion, drawn into Stephanie's improvised network of helpers.
characters.name: Dougie Kruper

recaps.ending: Stephanie confirms that Fred did not leave his family voluntarily: he was killed after his attention to the refuse business put him in the path of criminal activity. The apparently trivial dispute over a bill, the photographs and papers he left behind, and the people searching for the same information lead Stephanie to his body and to the danger that caused his disappearance. She survives the confrontation and closes the family's search with an answer, though not the one Mabel and Grandma Mazur wanted. Randy Briggs's failure-to-appear problem is also brought under control. Ranger's unexplained jobs have given Stephanie money and drawn her farther into his orbit, while Morelli remains her lover without a settled commitment. At the close, the attraction to both men is unresolved rather than converted into a choice, leaving the Ranger-Morelli triangle open.
recaps.in_short: Stephanie Plum takes on two very different searches: Vinnie's fugitive Randy Briggs and her missing Uncle Fred, a rigidly economical man last known to be disputing a refuse charge. Fred's disappearance leads through photographs, financial questions, the garbage business, and strangers who are also trying to recover what he found. Ranger supplements Stephanie's poor bounty income with secretive paid jobs, increasing the tension between her reliance on him and her continuing relationship with Joe Morelli. Lula, Grandma Mazur, Mooner, and Dougie help with the improvised investigation. Stephanie eventually learns that Fred uncovered criminal activity and was murdered rather than choosing to vanish. She finds the evidence and survives the people trying to suppress it, while the Briggs case is resolved separately. The professional cases close, but Stephanie's personal choice does not: Morelli remains her lover, Ranger remains an attractive and increasingly present alternative, and the book ends with that triangle deliberately unsettled.

recaps.text: Previously: Stephanie Plum became a Trenton apprehension agent by working for her cousin Vinnie's bail-bond office. Ranger trained her and remains her most dependable professional backup; Lula moved from the office into regular field work; and police officer Joe Morelli repeatedly shifted from former lover and rival to investigative ally. Stephanie's last case destroyed her apartment and pushed her into Morelli's home, turning their long-running attraction into an acknowledged sexual relationship without resolving what either expects from it. Ranger's close professional interest in Stephanie creates a second attraction that neither Morelli nor Stephanie can ignore.

Stephanie's aunt Mabel reports that Uncle Fred has disappeared after a characteristically stubborn argument over a refuse bill. Fred is predictable, careful with money, and not an obvious candidate to abandon his routines, so Stephanie agrees to make inquiries even though there is no bond fee attached. Her paying assignment is Randy Briggs, a computer programmer who failed to appear and has no intention of making his recovery easy. The two searches immediately show the difference between official bounty work and a family request: Briggs comes with a file, while Fred leaves only habits, relatives, and the remnants of his recent complaints.

Fred's trail widens beyond his argument over a bill. Photographs and papers suggest that he paid close attention to activity around the refuse business, while unfamiliar people show an interest in finding either Fred or something he possessed. Bunchy claims a financial reason to ask questions, but his persistence makes him another subject of Stephanie's investigation rather than a reliable source. Randy Briggs remains a separate practical problem, forcing Stephanie to improvise containment and protection instead of making a simple delivery to jail. Lula and Stephanie continue checking the people and places connected to Fred.

With bounty income unreliable, Stephanie accepts lucrative errands from Ranger. He provides little explanation, and the secrecy makes Morelli suspicious while increasing Stephanie's awareness of Ranger as more than a mentor. The work also gives her resources to continue Fred's case. Mooner and Dougie join the loose group of helpers around Stephanie, while the questions surrounding Fred become dangerous enough to rule out an innocent absence. The photographs and refuse-company connection now look less like an eccentric consumer complaint and more like evidence Fred encountered something others need concealed.

Stephanie follows the overlap among Fred's records, the garbage operation, and the people shadowing the search. Threats and interference confirm that Fred's disappearance is connected to criminal activity rather than a private decision to leave. Ranger and Morelli provide different forms of support, but each also presses on the unresolved limits of his relationship with Stephanie. The fugitive file on Randy Briggs continues alongside the family investigation, and Stephanie has to keep the manageable bond problem from distracting her from the increasingly likely prospect that Fred was killed for what he noticed.

The final search confirms that Uncle Fred was murdered after documenting suspicious activity connected to the refuse business. The bill dispute was only the visible beginning of a trail involving his photographs, the people trying to recover information, and the disposal system that helped conceal what happened. Stephanie reaches Fred's body and the evidence behind his disappearance, survives the attempt to stop her, and gives Mabel and Grandma Mazur a definite answer. Randy Briggs's failure-to-appear case is also brought under control. Ranger's paid work has drawn Stephanie closer to him, while her physical relationship with Morelli remains active but undefined. The cases end; the choice between the two men does not.

characters.description: Sixteen years old, already enormous and still growing, travelling on his own and stopping in New York City for a night in the summer of 1977. The son of a Marine, raised on bases around the world and schooled in fighting by his older brother and by circumstance, he has the West Point process ahead of him in the autumn. Literal-minded, curious about a city he does not know, and unable to walk past something he thinks is wrong, he intervenes when he sees a man beating a woman on a Greenwich Village street.
characters.name: Jack Reacher

characters.description: A local mafia operator who runs loan-sharking, protection and the rest of the neighbourhood's rackets, and who is used to nobody in it crossing him. Reacher first sees him beating a woman in the street, and the beating stops only because Reacher stops it - a humiliation Croselli has no intention of leaving unanswered.
characters.name: Croselli

characters.description: The woman Croselli was beating: an FBI agent whose career stalled when the case she built against him collapsed. Sidelined inside her own office and running out of chances, she is still working the man who ruined her, and a very large stranger who has just knocked him down in the street is the first help she has had in a long time.
characters.name: Jill Hemingway

characters.description: A college student with a car who falls in with Reacher by chance and spends the evening showing him a city he has never seen. She takes him at face value, treats the night as an adventure, and is with him when the lights go out.
characters.name: Chrissie

recaps.ending: Croselli is dead, killed by Reacher in his own blacked-out office after catching Hemingway and Reacher inside it. His hold on the neighbourhood dies with him, and Hemingway finally has the result she spent years failing to get, in a form no official report will account for cleanly. Chrissie comes through the night unhurt and goes back to her own life; she and Reacher part as what they were, two strangers who spent one interesting evening together. The power returns, and the blackout turns from a night people are living through into a story they tell. Reacher leaves New York the way he arrived, on his own and unremarked, with no charges, no consequences and nobody but Hemingway who knows exactly what he did, and goes back to his family and to the West Point process waiting for him in the autumn. The story closes as a piece of the character's prehistory: the first clear sight of the man the series' drifter becomes, at sixteen already deciding for himself what he will and will not walk past.
recaps.in_short: New York City, July 1977. Jack Reacher, sixteen years old and passing through on his own, sees a man beating a woman on a Greenwich Village street and stops it, hurting the man badly in the process. The man is Croselli, who runs the neighbourhood's rackets; the woman is Jill Hemingway, an FBI agent whose failed case against him wrecked her career. Reacher spends the evening with Chrissie, a student who drives him around a city he does not know, and then the power fails and New York goes dark, with looting and fires across the boroughs. Hemingway uses the blackout to go after the evidence in Croselli's office, and Reacher goes with her. Croselli, hunting the stranger who humiliated him, finds them there, and Reacher kills him. When the lights come back the neighbourhood is out from under him, and Reacher leaves the city unnoticed, with the army, the military police and a lifetime of drifting still ahead of him.

recaps.text: About this story: Jack Reacher is a former US Army military policeman who left the service and now drifts around America with no home, no luggage and no plans, walking into other people's trouble and dealing with it. This book is set long before any of that. It is a single night in New York City in July 1977, when Reacher was sixteen years old - a Marine's son raised on bases abroad, alone in the city for a day, with West Point ahead of him. Nothing else from the series is needed to follow it.

So far: Reacher, sixteen and on his own in New York on a hot July night, comes across a man beating a woman on a Greenwich Village street and steps in. He hurts the man enough to end it and walks away. The man is Croselli, who runs the neighbourhood's rackets and is not used to being touched; the woman is Jill Hemingway, an FBI agent whose case against Croselli collapsed and took her career with it. Reacher also falls in with Chrissie, a student with a car, and spends the evening being shown a city he has never seen. The city itself is on edge: a summer of heat, a serial killer the papers have made everyone afraid of, and a police force stretched thin. Croselli, who now knows there is a very large stranger loose in his streets, starts asking who he is.

So far: The power fails and the whole city goes dark. Looting and fires spread through the boroughs and the police effectively lose the streets. Hemingway sees the blackout as her one chance: what would prove Croselli's business is in his office, the alarms and lights are dead, and there will never be another night like it. Reacher, with nothing else to do and no intention of letting her try it alone, goes with her. Chrissie gets clear of the worst of it. Croselli, meanwhile, is out in the dark with his own men, protecting what is his and hunting the stranger who humiliated him, and the two searches converge on the same building.

So far: Hemingway and Reacher get into Croselli's office in the dark, and Croselli catches them there. The confrontation is settled in a blacked-out building with fists and a gun, and Reacher kills him. With Croselli dead the grip he had on the neighbourhood ends, and Hemingway is left with the outcome she had wanted for years, though not by any method she can write down. Chrissie is unhurt, and she and Reacher part as the strangers they were. When the lights come back on, Reacher walks out of the city as anonymously as he walked into it, sixteen years old, with the army, the military police and the drifting that follows all still in front of him.

characters.description: A medical-school lecturer living alone on the twenty-fifth floor after his divorce. Laing values the tower's privacy and controlled conveniences, and initially watches its social tensions with clinical detachment. He moves easily enough among its middle-level professionals without fully joining any camp.
characters.name: Robert Laing

characters.description: An architect who helped design the high-rise and occupies its penthouse. A past accident has left him with a damaged leg. Royal regards the building as an ambitious social experiment and identifies with the affluent residents of its upper floors.
characters.name: Anthony Royal

characters.description: A television producer who lives with his family on a lower floor. Physically forceful, restless, and conscious of the tower's class divisions, Wilder wants to document the mounting disorder and is increasingly drawn to the upper floors that exclude him.
characters.name: Richard Wilder

characters.description: Laing's neighbor and lover, who lives one floor above him with her young son. Charlotte is socially perceptive and more involved than Laing in the shifting alliances among residents, though she also tries to protect a workable private life inside the tower.
characters.name: Charlotte Melville

characters.description: Charlotte Melville's young son and one of the many children whose routines depend on the tower's schools, recreation areas, and elevators. His presence makes the adults' disputes over shared space more immediate for Charlotte and Laing.
characters.name: David Melville

characters.description: Richard Wilder's pregnant wife and the mother of their children. Helen is left to manage domestic life on the lower floors while her husband spends more time pursuing the tower's conflicts and his proposed film.
characters.name: Helen Wilder

characters.description: Anthony Royal's wife and a member of the tower's wealthy upper-floor circle. Anne shares the penthouse environment but is less invested than her husband in treating the building as a personal creation.
characters.name: Anne Royal

characters.description: Robert Laing's sister and another resident of the high-rise. Her family connection gives Laing an additional tie within the building even as both become absorbed in its increasingly self-contained life.
characters.name: Alice Laing

characters.description: A physician among the high-rise's upper-level residents. Pangbourne belongs to Royal's social group and becomes involved in its efforts to control territory and movement as ordinary neighborly relations deteriorate.
characters.name: Pangbourne

recaps.ending: The high-rise becomes almost completely cut off from ordinary city life. Services have failed, apartments have been stripped, and the remaining residents organize themselves into small territorial groups while accepting violence as routine. Wilder finally completes his obsessive climb from the lower floors to the roof and confronts Royal. Both men are killed in the final violence after Wilder reaches the summit he had pursued. Laing survives by adapting to the building's new order. He settles into a closed domestic arrangement with women nearby, scavenges what remains, and eats one of the tower's dogs. He has no wish to call for outside help or resume his former life. Looking from his balcony, he notices disturbances beginning in another tower in the development, suggesting that the same collapse is spreading beyond his own building.
recaps.in_short: A new forty-storey residential tower promises affluent tenants a self-sufficient life of apartments, shops, schools, pools, and private recreation. Medical lecturer Robert Laing lives near its middle, architect Anthony Royal occupies the penthouse, and television producer Richard Wilder lives with his family below. Small failures of elevators, power, and shared facilities sharpen the building's class divisions. Parties, vandalism, raids, and assaults replace complaints, while residents conceal the disorder from outsiders and withdraw from work. Wilder becomes obsessed with climbing and filming the tower; Royal tries to preserve upper-floor control; Laing discovers that he prefers the enclosed, increasingly primitive community. As services collapse, residents form territorial groups and abandon ordinary restraints. Wilder reaches the roof, and both he and Royal die in the final violence. Laing remains willingly inside, eating a dog and watching signs that a neighboring high-rise is beginning the same descent.

recaps.text: Three months after moving into a new forty-storey high-rise outside London, medical lecturer Robert Laing has settled into a life designed to minimize contact with the world beyond the building. The tower contains shops, schools, pools, and recreation decks, and its residents sort themselves informally by height and income. Laing occupies the middle levels and spends time with his neighbor Charlotte Melville. Architect Anthony Royal, who helped design the complex, lives in the penthouse and views it as a social experiment. Television producer Richard Wilder lives with his pregnant wife Helen and their children on a lower floor. Minor power failures, delayed elevators, noise, and competition over shared facilities begin producing quarrels between floors. Wilder recognizes an emerging conflict between the lower, middle, and upper residents, while Laing remains attracted to the tower's impersonal order and watches its tensions without trying to leave.

The tower's inconveniences turn into deliberate provocations. Residents crowd parties, damage communal areas, and retaliate against neighbors from other levels. A dog is found drowned in a swimming pool, making clear that the conflict has moved beyond arguments over noise and elevators. Royal and the upper-floor residents defend their privileged territory, while Wilder grows determined to record the building and force his way upward. Laing participates in the parties and shifting alliances rather than seeking outside intervention. When a resident falls to his death, the building has crossed into lethal disorder. Yet the tenants close ranks, treat the event as an internal matter, and continue going to work while hiding the scale of the breakdown. Their shared secrecy allows the high-rise to become a world with its own rules.

Failures of power, water, elevators, and refuse collection spread through the building. Instead of cooperating, tenants raid rival floors for food and equipment, barricade corridors, and use stairwells and service routes to defend territory. The three broad social zones split into smaller clans centered on particular floors and apartments. Wilder neglects Helen and the children as his projected documentary becomes an obsession with reaching the top. Royal tries to maintain the authority of the penthouse group, although his control is increasingly symbolic. Laing stops treating the crisis as temporary. He misses work, gathers supplies, and finds the building's closed and violent life more compelling than the orderly professional identity he had outside. Contact with the surrounding city continues, but the residents make little effort to obtain help and actively conceal what is happening.

The residents abandon most of their former routines. Apartments are invaded and stripped, animals disappear, and the darkened corridors are marked by refuse and wreckage. Groups conduct raids between floors and absorb isolated tenants, while women and children form their own defensive arrangements. Royal is injured and loses much of his ability to direct the upper levels, but remains attached to the structure he designed. Wilder continues his upward campaign, treating each floor crossed as an advance against the building's hierarchy. Laing adapts with less resistance. He secures his apartment, forages through neighboring rooms, and accepts relationships organized around immediate protection rather than ordinary social obligations. The tower's physical decline and the residents' psychological retreat reinforce each other, leaving little distinction between a broken service system and a chosen rejection of outside life.

The high-rise is now a collection of hostile enclaves. Few residents attend their jobs, and those still inside have stopped expecting repairs or rescue. Food, water, and defensible rooms determine movement. Royal's penthouse position no longer guarantees command; his injured body and the collapse of the upper-floor coalition mirror the failure of his architectural ideal. Wilder, increasingly detached from Helen and his former purpose as a filmmaker, presses toward the roof with single-minded determination. Laing has become comfortable inside the new order and does not regard a return to normal life as desirable. He moves among nearby apartments, scavenges, and joins a small domestic group. Violence continues, but it is no longer experienced by the remaining tenants as an interruption. It has become the organizing condition of life in the tower.

The building completes its separation from the city. Its services are ruined, its former class structure has fragmented, and the survivors live in small groups among looted apartments and dead animals. Wilder finally reaches the highest levels and confronts Royal, fulfilling his long campaign to overcome the hierarchy embodied by the tower. Royal is killed during the final violence, and Wilder also dies after attaining the summit. Their opposing efforts to master the building end together. Laing survives because he has ceased trying to master or reform it. He accepts a confined arrangement with women in neighboring apartments, scavenges food, and cooks one of the remaining dogs. The opening image of him eating on his balcony is thus revealed as the settled condition toward which the previous months have moved. Laing feels no urgency to summon help. From the tower he sees lights flickering irregularly in another high-rise nearby and recognizes the first signs of a similar breakdown beginning there.

characters.description: The consulting detective of Baker Street, represented here at several points in his later career. Holmes combines close observation, disguise, specialist knowledge, and carefully planned action when clients or public officials bring him difficult problems.
characters.name: Sherlock Holmes

characters.description: Holmes's physician friend, former army surgeon, and customary chronicler. Watson remains a loyal companion in investigations separated by years, preserving both Holmes's reasoning and the circumstances in which the cases arise.
characters.name: John H. Watson

characters.description: The landlady associated with Holmes's rooms at 221B Baker Street. Mrs Hudson's care for Holmes and management of the household place her close to the unusual visitors, disguises, and alarms that accompany his work.
characters.name: Mrs Hudson

characters.description: Sherlock Holmes's older brother, whose extraordinary memory and analytical ability serve the British government. Mycroft turns to Sherlock when a matter of national importance requires active investigation outside his own habits and office.
characters.name: Mycroft Holmes

characters.description: A Scotland Yard inspector who has worked with Holmes before. Lestrade brings the authority and resources of the police to investigations in which Holmes is asked to provide an independent reading of the evidence.
characters.name: Inspector Lestrade

recaps.ending: The title story takes place on the eve of Britain's entry into the First World War. Holmes has spent two years under the identity of the Irish-American Altamont, earning the confidence of the German agent Von Bork and feeding his network misleading intelligence. At Von Bork's country house, Holmes arrives with Watson, reveals the deception, and takes Von Bork prisoner along with the agent's papers. Their work completed, Holmes and Watson leave to deliver the captive and evidence to the authorities. Holmes has come out of retirement for this national assignment, while Watson has again joined him in the field. The closing conversation turns from the successful operation to the war approaching Britain, giving the collection a public and historical conclusion rather than the private solution of an ordinary Baker Street case.
recaps.in_short: This later collection gathers independent cases from different stages of Holmes and Watson's association, including investigations involving government secrets, unusual illnesses, disappearances, foreign connections, and dangers concealed within apparently private affairs. Mycroft Holmes, Inspector Lestrade, and Mrs Hudson return alongside the two central partners. Editions differ over whether "The Cardboard Box" belongs here or in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, but the remaining stories form the stable core. The final and only continuing endpoint is the title story, set in August 1914. Holmes has left retirement to spend two years posing as the agent Altamont and infiltrating the German spy Von Bork's network. With Watson's help, he exposes the disguise, captures Von Bork, and secures the agent's papers for Britain. The partners depart together as the country stands at the beginning of war, closing the volume on national service rather than another private case.

recaps.text: Collection scope: "Wisteria Lodge," "The Red Circle," "The Bruce-Partington Plans," "The Dying Detective," "The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax," "The Devil's Foot," and "His Last Bow" form the collection's stable group of self-contained stories. Many editions also include "The Cardboard Box," which other editions place in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes. The cases range across Holmes's later career; the title story is a distinct wartime epilogue rather than the solution to a collection-wide mystery.
